section_1.title: Introduction: The Chaos of the Coffee Cup
section_1.content: Briefly introduce the phenomenon of turbulence using the analogy of cream swirling in a cup of coffee. Define turbulence as non-linear, multi-scale motion and establish the Reynolds number (Re) as the prerequisite non-dimensional parameter that dictates transition to chaos.
section_1.example: Visualizing cream eddies: A small stir (low Re) leads to smooth streamlines; a rapid stir (high Re) creates a hierarchy of swirling structures.

section_2.title: The Kolmogorov Cascade: Energy Transfer
section_2.content: Explain Richardson’s cascade: large eddies break into smaller ones, transferring kinetic energy down to the viscous scale. Introduce the energy spectrum E(k) ~ k^(-5/3) as the 'DNA' of turbulence.
section_2.example: An animated 'Russian Nesting Doll' model where large vortices (parent) spawn smaller, faster-spinning vortices (children) until friction dissipates the energy.

section_3.title: The Kolmogorov Constant (C): A Universal Signature
section_3.content: Introduce Kolmogorov’s hypothesis of local isotropy. The constant 'C' (~1.5) appears in the spectrum formula: E(k) = C * ε^(2/3) * k^(-5/3). Emphasize that this constant is universal, regardless of the fluid.
section_3.example: A comparison animation: Turbulence in a mountain stream vs. turbulence in the atmosphere of Jupiter, both collapsing onto the same -5/3 slope graph.

section_4.title: Mathematical Structure: The Dissipation Scale
section_4.content: Define the Kolmogorov length scale η (eta). This is the 'mathematical cliff' where viscosity dominates and kinetic energy is converted to heat, ending the mathematical structure of the cascade.
section_4.example: An animation of a 'Tornado' character shrinking down; at the macro-scale, it's a storm, but as it reaches scale η, it flattens and vanishes into a 'thermal glow'.

section_5.title: Summary & Real-World Application
section_5.content: Synthesize how these constants allow engineers to predict drag and mixing without solving every tiny vortex. Recap: Re defines the regime, k^(-5/3) defines the structure, and η defines the limit.
section_5.example: Designing an aircraft wing: Using the -5/3 law to estimate how the 'turbulent noise' around the wing affects fuel efficiency.
